name: Test booster blends (Prime Male, TestoFuel)

lead: Test booster blends such as Prime Male and TestoFuel combine herbs, vitamins and minerals and are marketed to raise or support testosterone. Users hope for more muscle, energy and a leaner body composition.

Marketing says the ingredients support the body's own testosterone production or reduce its conversion or binding. No published trial of either named product was found; research on single ingredients is inconsistent, and Wikipedia states that Tribulus terrestris did not consistently affect testosterone in controlled studies.

paras: They are taken as daily capsules or powders bought online, usually on top of a training and diet plan. Users commonly run a bottle or two and compare energy, gym progress and bloodwork.

Supplement blends are sold without prior approval for effectiveness, and ingredients and interactions vary by product. The Australian Institute of Sport, cited by Wikipedia, discourages athletes from using Tribulus supplements, citing no good evidence of effectiveness or safety.

angle.text: Test booster blends combine herbs and vitamins that are marketed to raise testosterone, for more muscle and a leaner body. They are sold online and discussed in looksmaxxing forums. No published trial of these specific products was found.

lead: Test booster blends are multi-ingredient dietary supplements marketed to raise or support testosterone, usually combining amino acids, herbal extracts, vitamins and minerals. Prime Male and TestoFuel are two brands sold online, mainly through their own websites. People take them hoping for the physique and energy associated with higher testosterone: more muscle, easier training recovery, leaner body composition and better drive in the gym.

The chain users describe is: ingredients nudge the body's own testosterone production or availability, training capacity improves, and muscle gain and leanness follow. Brand formulations are set by the manufacturers and change over time, so the label is the source for ingredients. Common ingredients in this product category include zinc, fenugreek, vitamin B6, Tribulus terrestris, magnesium, boron, D-aspartic acid and ashwagandha [1].

No published clinical trial of Prime Male or TestoFuel as products was found. A 2020 analysis of 50 products sold as testosterone boosters found that 90 percent claimed to boost testosterone, while about a quarter of the ingredients had published data showing an increase [1]. Wikipedia states that Tribulus did not consistently affect testosterone in controlled studies [2], and its ashwagandha article notes that the herb may raise testosterone levels, with rare reports of liver injury [3].
infobox: Zinc, fenugreek, vitamin B6, Tribulus, magnesium, boron, D-aspartic acid, ashwagandha (varies by brand) [1]
Sold as dietary supplements; the FDA does not approve them for effectiveness

paras: Blends differ by brand and product version, so current labels list what each contains. Tribulus terrestris has been used in supplements since the 1980s on the belief that it raises testosterone [2]. Ashwagandha is sold as root or leaf powder or extract [3]. Fenugreek is sold as capsules, powder, tea and extract in many countries [4].

The category covers dozens of brands that share a marketing promise but differ in formulation. In a 2020 review in the World Journal of Men's Health, Clemesha and colleagues catalogued 50 products found through a Google search for "testosterone booster". The products contained 109 unique ingredients, averaging 8.3 per product; 90 percent of the products claimed to boost testosterone, 50 percent claimed improved libido and 48 percent claimed users would feel stronger [1].

Zinc appeared in 64.4 percent of the products, fenugreek extract in 48.9 percent, Tribulus in 42.2 percent, D-aspartic acid in 20 percent and ashwagandha in 17.8 percent [5]. Thirteen products exceeded the FDA upper tolerable intake level for zinc, vitamin B3 or magnesium, and median doses of vitamins B12, B6, zinc, B5 and B3 were far above the recommended daily allowance [1]. The authors note that the FDA states supplements are not intended to treat or cure disease, yet most products carried testosterone claims [5].

Wikipedia reports that Tribulus did not consistently affect testosterone in controlled studies and that no reviews show strength-enhancing effects [2]. Its ashwagandha article says the herb may raise testosterone, which could matter for people on certain cancer medicines [3]. Its fenugreek article describes studies as mostly small and of limited quality and says the US FDA has not approved fenugreek for clinical use [4].

In the 2020 analysis, a PubMed search for each ingredient found that 24.8 percent of ingredients had data showing increased testosterone, 18.3 percent showed no change, 10.1 percent showed a decrease and 61.5 percent had no data; some ingredients, including D-aspartic acid, appear in more than one category because studies conflict [1][5]. A 2023 randomized trial of 16 male boxers in simulated altitude found that D-aspartic acid at six grams a day for 14 days did not significantly change resting testosterone or the testosterone-to-cortisol ratio [1]. A 2026 study of a different, company-affiliated herbal blend reported higher testosterone and strength gains than placebo over 60 days of resistance training in healthy men, along with increases in rats; its authors are affiliated with the manufacturer [1].

Ashwagandha has been linked to rare herb-induced liver injury, most often in people with existing liver conditions, plus diarrhea, headache, sedation and nausea; it is advised against in pregnancy and hormone-sensitive prostate cancer [3]. Fenugreek can cause digestive upset, a maple-like body odor and low blood sugar, and may interact with diabetes and anticoagulant drugs [4]. The Australian Institute of Sport discourages athletes from using Tribulus supplements [2].

sections.h: What marketed blends claim and contain
paras: The 2020 descriptive study by Clemesha and colleagues searched for the term testosterone booster, took the first 50 products returned, and compared their labels with PubMed research on each ingredient.[5] Ninety percent of products claimed to raise testosterone or free testosterone, 62 percent claimed to build lean or muscle mass, 50 percent claimed more libido and 48 percent claimed greater strength; some also claimed fat burning, faster recovery or anti-estrogen effects.[5]

The products held 109 distinct ingredients, averaging about eight per product, most commonly zinc, fenugreek, vitamin B6, Tribulus and magnesium.[5] Vitamin and mineral amounts were often well above recommended daily values, with median levels of about 1,291 percent of the daily value for vitamin B12, 808 percent for vitamin B6 and 272 percent for zinc, and some products exceeded upper tolerable limits for zinc, vitamin B3 and magnesium.[5]

Of the 109 ingredients, 27 had published data showing a testosterone increase, 11 had data showing a decrease, 20 showed no change, 15 had conflicting results and 67 had no studies.[5] The authors cite a case report of pulmonary embolism linked to a fenugreek-containing testosterone supplement and a study in which red clover was associated with raised liver enzymes, and note that excess zinc can interfere with copper and iron absorption.[5] They conclude that most claims lacked supporting research and that consumers may not be getting ingredients to support them, while noting their study was limited to one search engine, one search term and 50 products.[5]

Brands such as Prime Male and TestoFuel are marketed to men for energy, drive and training performance, and the appeal for appearance is the chain from higher testosterone to more muscle, leaner body composition and stronger workouts.[6][1] Because formulations change, product labels are the authoritative list of ingredients.
No studies found of Prime Male or TestoFuel as products.

Ingredient-level research is inconsistent for Tribulus [2], limited in quality for fenugreek [4], and mixed for D-aspartic acid, which has data showing both increases and no change in different studies [1][1]. A 2020 product-composition analysis found that 24.8 percent of the ingredients across 50 products had supporting testosterone data [1].

Testosterone-focused forums such as T Nation discuss test boosters often. One member who used a mild booster reported worse sleep, which surprised him since zinc is a common ingredient [6]. Another posted lab results after stopping boosters and adding vitamin D and boron, reporting lower total and free testosterone [7]. Others ask whether any boosters work [8]. Such posts are individual reports.

Testosterone-booster supplements are sold in the US as dietary supplements, a category that does not require FDA approval for effectiveness before sale [5]. Sales are largely online, and brands frequently rely on review sites and affiliate marketing, which the forum discussion treats with varying degrees of trust.

lore.intro: On T Nation and similar forums, test boosters are discussed both as a first step before prescription therapy and as something members question.

claims.claim: Over-the-counter test boosters raise testosterone enough to help muscle gain.
Boosters made from common ingredients such as zinc improve sleep and recovery.
Test boosters work as a legal, safer alternative to prescription testosterone.
